DcG4bUVtRFU.caption:
persancte on August 16, 2026: "SSS_0026_01 // Modelled in Blender. Rendered in Blender 5.2 using the Khronos PBR Color Space.

Symmetry appears throughout the natural world. It shapes faces, animal bodies, flowers, leaves and many other biological structures. We recognize these patterns almost immediately, and in faces especially, symmetry often contributes to our perception of balance and beauty.

But natural symmetry is never exact. Both sides of a face, a leaf or an animal may follow the same underlying structure while still carrying small differences. Growth, development and environmental conditions constantly introduce variation. The result is order without mathematical perfection.

Natural materials behave with a similar complexity. Light does not always stop at the surface. It can enter a material, scatter beneath it and return somewhere else. This is especially visible in skin, leaves, fruit, wax and other organic matter, but more subtle forms of internal light transport also occur in materials such as wood. It is one of the reasons natural surfaces can feel soft, deep and physically present.

These principles are deliberately intensified throughout SSS. Symmetry becomes more pronounced, while small irregularities remain. Translucency and subsurface scattering exaggerate material depth. Color relationships are pushed beyond ordinary perception, amplifying variations that exist in nature but are often too subtle to consciously notice.

Scale is treated in the same way. A structure may suggest tissue, a plant surface or part of an animal, while its actual size remains uncertain. Familiar biological qualities are removed from their usual context and given a different spatial presence.

The aim is not to reproduce nature literally, but to isolate some of the visual principles through which we recognize it in the first place.".

_cinearts_ on July 25, 2026: "The Club of the Laid Off (Klub odložených, 1989) is one of the most distinctive films in Labyrinth of Darkness, the anthology collecting Jiří Barta's darker and more experimental stop-motion works. Moving away from the refined aesthetic of traditional Eastern European puppet animation, Barta based the film on a highly physical production process that emphasized the material qualities of both the puppets and the sets.
Rather than building new models, the production sourced antique mannequins made of wood, wax, and papier-mâché alongside modern plastic figures. Since these mannequins were never designed for animation, their limbs had to be manually cut, re-jointed, and adapted to create even the simplest movements, resulting in the film's deliberately rigid, mechanical motion. Shot over several months under hot studio lights, the figures gradually accumulated real cracks, worn paint, and surface damage, allowing the effects of time to become part of the animation itself.
The film contains no dialogue, relying instead on image and sound to shape its atmosphere. Cinematographer Ivan Vít carefully adjusted the lighting frame by frame to recreate subtle changes in the attic environment, while the soundtrack was built from recorded creaking wood, snapping plastic, and grinding joints. The result is a form of stop-motion in which the physical properties of the materials are as expressive as the animation itself.

In July 1980, British post-punk group The Cure made a memorable television appearance on the Dutch music program TROS Top 50 to promote material from their second studio album, Seventeen Seconds. Recorded at the Hilversum studio alongside keyboardist Matthieu Hartley and drummer Lol Tolhurst, the cheeky performance showcased the band's playful resistance toward conventional music promotion during a key transitional era in their career.

The tape sat in the archives for decades before being officially rediscovered in the vaults of Dutch public broadcaster AVROTROS and restored for full release. At the time of the original broadcast, The Cure was rapidly evolving from their sparse post-punk roots into the atmospheric, darker soundscapes that defined 1980s gothic rock, propelled by the breakthrough success of their hit single A Forest. That track, which peaked at number 31 on the UK Singles Chart and broke into the Dutch Top 40, marked the band's first major commercial milestone. 30K likes, 129 comments - harr.ysalce on June 4, 2026: "GOLDEN RATIO to build COLOR PALLETES from one color…

Example poster by Sanzuan 

FULL FORMULA: 

Step 1: Pick a main color
For this example I used: 008CBB

Step 2: Find your accent color using the Golden Angle
The Golden Ratio is: 1.618

To find the Golden Angle:
360 ÷ 1.618 = 222.5
360 − 222.5 = 137.5°

Now move 137.5° around the color wheel from your original color.
That gives me: FFC20F
This becomes my accent color.

Step 3: Create a support color
Take your original color: 008CBB
Reduce its saturation by roughly 60%
Which gives: A1C5D1

Final Palette
Primary: 008CBB
Support: A1C5D1
Accent: FFC20F".
